summary: Egle Monitor is a technical software and interface proposal for long-duration space missions that centralizes astronaut physiology, internal habitat conditions, and radiation levels using validated NASA hardware. Powered by edge computing, the system anticipates adverse clinical evenhttps://canva.link/bvt1wbnb8pd4ht0ts and executes automated prevention and response protocols to manage medical complications without relying entirely on mission control or online connection.
details:
When a medical or environmental crisis unfolds in orbit or on a transit to Mars, astronauts cannot wait for terrestrial doctors or decipher convoluted software. We built EGLE MONITOR to maintain uninterrupted, real-time medical statistics for all crew members at all times alongside continuous cabin life-support telemetry, turning complex clinical data into immediate action. From arrival in orbit, our platform compares live physiological and environmental readings against each astronaut's pre-flight baseline. Whenever any metric drifts toward danger, EGLE MONITOR alerts the astronaut, crew, and command center so subtle signs like early dehydration, rising CO2, or cumulative radiation are caught before becoming fatal emergencies.

What makes our project essential for deep-space exploration is its universal readability regardless of a crew member's medical preparation. Under NASA standards, spacecraft carry Crew Medical Officers who in Low-Earth Orbit are often trained only as Emergency Medical Technicians, and on lunar or Martian missions, communication delays prevent real-time guidance from Earth flight surgeons. True Earth independence means any astronaut—pilot, engineer, or scientist—can glance at the console during an emergency, immediately understand what is wrong, and execute the protocol to save a crewmate. We rejected dark, cluttered sci-fi graphics that obscure numbers under stress, instead crafting a high-contrast, analog-inspired modular workstation interface modeled on classic industrial window managers. Crisp beveled panels, recessed digital readouts, linear analog range gauges, and clear green, yellow, and red indicators strip away ambiguity so anyone can read vital statistics and follow plain-English emergency protocols in seconds.

Architecturally, we evolved EGLE MONITOR from a deterministic Python and Tkinter telemetry engine into a responsive web application built with React, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, and Lucide-React, split into two dedicated workspaces. In Astronaut Health, operators track seven physiological and behavioral variables—Blood Sugar, Blood Pressure, Heart Rate, Personal Radiation, Sleep Hours, Mood, and Core Body Temperature—by clicking an interactive anatomical sensor map or selecting any telemetry tile to view multi-day trends and step-by-step clinical protocols. In Habitat Environment, four life-support metrics—Cabin Temperature, Carbon Dioxide, Oxygen, and Intra- versus Extra-Vehicular Radiation—appear with linear range bars and plain-English corrective checklists requiring zero specialized training to interpret.

We invite the judges to look deep beneath our interface into the extensive aerospace and biomedical research powering every threshold, equation, and protocol. We obtained the vast majority of our data and limits directly from NASA open-source files and public technical repositories, synthesizing NASA-STD-3001 Volumes 1 and 2, OCHMO Technical Briefs, and IECLSSIS life-support standards. For core thermometry, we integrated Steinhart-Hart thermistor calibration equations alongside ISS Thermolab and Thermo-Mini open-source findings on space fever, accounting for how missing natural convection and an 11 percent drop in evaporative sweat cooling in microgravity make core temperature rise faster during exercise and cool slower afterward. Our cardiovascular module models oscillometric Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP = DBP + (SBP - DBP) / 3) while enforcing microgravity emergency rules, warning crew not to elevate a hypotensive astronaut's legs as on Earth due to cephalad fluid shift. Every clinical rule shares this rigor: hypoglycemia alerts below 70 mg/dL guide conscious crew to ingest 15 grams of fast-acting carbs and re-test in 15 minutes while forbidding oral intake if unconscious, and hypothermia alerts below 35 degrees Celsius prohibit direct heat or rapid rewarming.

This NASA open-source research also powers our radiation, atmospheric, and behavioral modules. We convert absorbed dose rates in microGray per hour to dose equivalents in mSv/h using Q(LET), switch from 90-second to 20-second FAST sampling during solar spikes, and track cumulative exposure against NASA's 250 mSv short-term and 600 mSv career limits. To prevent alarm flickering, our shelter protocol uses hysteresis: above 1.0 mSv/h, crew relocate to the shielded central core until rates drop below 0.10 mSv/h. Environmentally, we monitor 1-hour rolling CO2 (< 3.0 mmHg), oxygen partial pressure with at least 30 percent diluent gas, and cabin temperature (18–27 °C), while cross-referencing PHQ-9, GAD-7, POMS, and sleep actigraphy with cabin conditions. Finally, our top-bar Threshold Simulator lets judges and crew cycle live through nominal, advisory, and critical states, proving EGLE MONITOR functions as both a mission-critical console and an onboard training tool for autonomous spaceflight.
